newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria's industrial output sags further.
newsitem.headline: Algeria's industrial output sags further.

text.p: Algeria's industrial production, hit by shortages of spares, raw materials and falling demand, worsened in the last quarter of 1996 to cap a year when output fell seven percent overall.
The National Statistics Office said on Wednesday that the core manufacturing industries notched up an even worse drop of 12.9 percent over the year compared to 1995.
Overall, Algeria's economy has been growing by around four percent annually for the past three years, reversing stagnation of the previous decade.
But the latest figures underline the continuing crisis in industry in the North African country which relies on oil and gas exports for about 95 percent of foreign earnings.
The figures, carried by the official Algerian news agency APS, showed output fell 9.7 percent in the last quarter of 1996 with manufacturing showing the worst slump, of 16.1 percent.
Output in 1995 contracted 0.5 percent after an eight percent fall the year before.
The continued slump in 1996 underlined problems faced by Algeria in its efforts to save industry as a major employer while switching to a free market after nearly three decades of state control.
Officials in Algeria, shaken by more than five years of violence, have blamed unemployment and poverty for adding to the ranks of Moslem rebels trying to topple the authorities.

Algeria's macro-economic reforms have won praise from financial institutions and produced foreign reserves of over $5 billion at the end of 1996. But there is continuing alarm over the state of industry.
Earlier this week, a semi-official think tank said the social situation of ordinary Algerians was worsening and there was continued stagnation of the non-oil and gas industry.
"Industrial activity is still in the recessionary stage and the (government) objectives have not been achieved," said the Social and Economic National Council.
Algeria's oil and gas exports earned some $12.6 billion in 1996. But it has been trying to boost industry with the aim of achieving $2 billion in non-energy exports by the year 2000 and saving jobs.

Around two million people are unemployed with an active workforce of some six million, and many of the 400 state enterprises -- more than half of which the country is trying to privatise -- are overmanned and inefficient.

The statistics office said that besides lack of spare parts for industrial machinery and semi-finished materials, factory output had been hit by debt problems, some competition from imported goods, and by a drop in demand.

Last Monday, Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia told a news conference in Algiers: "The most important thing is to preserve the production tool which has been hit by the crisis up to 1996, particularly the industrial sector."
He said that only about 47 non-energy state enterprises, employing 71,000 people, could afford to meet a pay rise being sought by the unions.
"If we decide a pay increases of five or 10 percent for example, we are going to break the productive apparatus and the end result will be the closure of the enterprises..," he said.

The statistics office said production in the farm-food industries had shrunk 9.3 percent in the last quarter of 1996, with an overall fall of four percent in output of the farm produce industry for the whole year.

Algeria is one of the world's main importers of cereals to feed its 29 million people, and Ouyahia on Monday said food imports at the end of 1996 were the country's biggest import expense. This had, however, now dropped to second place after imports of equipment, he said.
